frameworks.name: Three Reality Distortions (Ellis-Hormozi)
frameworks.definition: Adapted from Albert Ellis's CBT framework: the three irrational beliefs that cause people to cast power away from themselves — Circumstances (I must get what I want when I want it), Others (people must treat me fairly or be condemned), and Self (I must do well or I am no good) — which manifest in sales as time, money, fit, authority, and avoidance objections.

frameworks.name: Five Objection Categories (Hormozi)
frameworks.definition: The five surface manifestations of the three reality distortions in a sales context: Time (busy, bad timing), Value/Price (too expensive, can't afford), Fit (not for me, wrong vehicle), Authority (need spouse/partner approval), and Avoidance/Stall (need to think about it). Ordered from surface-level to core self.

frameworks.name: Three Closing Questions (Hormozi)
frameworks.definition: The core close after all external objections are exhausted: (1) Do you believe this product will help you achieve your goal? (2) Do you trust me to fulfill my word? (3) Do you believe it will work for you specifically? When all three are yes, close on access to money.

frameworks.name: Obstacle vs. Objection Distinction
frameworks.definition: Obstacles are disagreements that surface before asking for the sale; objections arise after the sale is solicited. Obstacles are easier to handle because no stake has been presented yet; they should be fully resolved before entering closing mode.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the top five red-zone offenses in the NFL made the playoffs 90% of the time over the prior five years — and uses this as an analogy for closing skill: mastery of closing alone compensates for significant deficiencies elsewhere in a sales process or business.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: early-stage businesses where founder is the primary closer
claims.mechanism: Closing converts qualified attention into revenue; without it, all upstream marketing and lead generation produces no return.

numbers.axis: playoff rate by red-zone offense quality

bounded_by: Does not imply closing alone replaces all other skills long-term — only buys time to build them

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that of any 100 prospects entering a sales process, 10% will never buy regardless of execution, 10% will always buy and require no persuasion, and the middle 80% is where closing skill determines the outcome.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: general service or coaching offers with an explicit sales conversation

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that selling is a transference of belief over a bridge of trust, and therefore two conditions must both be present for a sale to close: the seller must genuinely believe in the product, and the prospect must trust the seller. A sales cold streak is almost always caused by loss of belief rather than loss of skill.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: transference of belief over a bridge of trust
conditions: high-touch consultative sales
seller is the primary closer
claims.mechanism: Belief is the content being transferred; trust is the channel. If either is absent — even with perfect technique — the transfer fails because the seller's unconscious signals betray the deficit.
bounded_by: Does not apply to transactional self-serve purchases where the seller has no direct interaction

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that humans are exceptionally good at detecting whether a salesperson genuinely wants to help them or is motivated only by closing the deal — and that sellers who care only about the close cannot build the trust necessary to close consistently.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Intent detection is a survival mechanism; people evolved to spot those who would double-cross them. The cognitive mismatch between stated and actual motive leaks through micro-signals that prospects read subconsciously.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that if a seller is not getting gasps from their price reveal, they have not gone high enough, and they forfeit the anchoring advantage: stating a $100,000 price first makes a $1,000 price feel like a rounding error, whereas stating $10 first makes $1,000 feel large.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: in-person or live-call sales conversation where price is revealed verbally
claims.mechanism: The high anchor recalibrates the prospect's reference point; all subsequent prices are evaluated relative to the anchor, not in absolute terms.

numbers.axis: anchor price vs. subsequent price perception

bounded_by: Does not apply to transparent-price ecommerce or subscription contexts where price is displayed before any conversation

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that closing is a dance, not a fight — the goal is to sell from your back foot, signaling genuine willingness to let the prospect walk away, which paradoxically reduces prospect resistance and increases close rates.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: consultative sales with explicit close conversation
claims.mechanism: High-pressure attempts signal desperation, which prospects interpret as evidence the product lacks intrinsic value. Detachment signals abundance and confidence, both of which raise perceived product value.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a seller who shifts their success metric from 'did I make the sale' to 'did I help the prospect make a decision to help themselves' eliminates performance anxiety and paradoxically increases close rates, because the seller can win on every conversation regardless of whether money changes hands.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: seller genuinely believes the product helps the prospect
claims.mechanism: Changing the metric removes the emotional stake that causes hesitation and high-pressure behavior. The seller can then ask hard questions and stay curious without fear, which prospect perceive as genuine care — the actual driver of trust.
bounded_by: Requires that the seller genuinely believes in the product; faked detachment does not produce the same effect

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that objections to time ('I'm too busy', 'not a good time') are overcome by pointing out that the prospect will continue to be busy forever, so beginning a habit or program during a busy period is the only way to ensure it sticks — learning a skill during ideal conditions means it will fail when conditions become difficult again.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prospect claims busyness as the reason for not buying a program or service
claims.mechanism: Skills learned only under favorable conditions are conditional; skills learned under adverse conditions generalize to all conditions.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that 'when-then' thinking (when I have X, then I will do Y) is a logical fallacy that inverts causal sequence — people plan to save money once they're rich, buy the fitness program once they have a six-pack, or invest in education once they have more time — and that surfacing the fallacy explicitly is enough to dissolve the objection in many cases.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prospect states they will begin when a prerequisite condition is met
claims.mechanism: The when-then pattern applies the output of a process as the prerequisite for entering the process, creating a logical impossibility. Once made explicit with absurd examples (save money once I'm rich), the prospect cannot defend it rationally.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that when a prospect says a price is too much money, this is actually a reason they are more likely to succeed — because a higher perceived sacrifice increases commitment, which increases program completion rates.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prospect has verbally acknowledged the price feels significant
buying a results-based program
claims.mechanism: Skin in the game increases follow-through; people who perceive they have paid a meaningful amount self-select into higher engagement to justify the cost.
bounded_by: Does not apply if the absolute price is genuinely beyond the prospect's liquidity — the argument works only when the price is a stretch, not impossible

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that prospects who cite money as the objection have effectively revealed it is not about money — because once they agree the value would be there if the product delivered results, the real barrier is belief in the outcome, not the price itself.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prospect has agreed the outcome would be valuable if the product works
claims.mechanism: Agreeing to value-if-delivered while refusing to pay surfaces that the core obstacle is trust or belief, not price — which allows the seller to redirect to the actual issue.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that money spent on education is a time purchase: prospects will learn the lessons in a program either through the program (12 weeks) or through unaided trial-and-error (12 years), and the program price is the cost of buying the experiential knowledge of thousands of predecessors who already paid in time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prospect objects to price of a skill-building or results program
claims.mechanism: Human civilization accelerates by buying accumulated lessons rather than re-deriving them; individual actors who pay for others' mistake-derived knowledge bypass the original time cost.

numbers.axis: time to learn skill independently vs. via program

bounded_by: Requires the program to actually contain distilled learnable lessons; does not hold for low-content premium-priced products

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that resourcefulness, not resources, is what separates self-made wealthy individuals from everyone else — pointing out that every self-made billionaire started with zero, so the starting position of having no money is not a distinguishing constraint.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prospect or person claims lack of capital as a barrier to starting or investing
bounded_by: Does not account for structural access barriers beyond capital (e.g., regulatory licensing, geography, health); claim is strongest for knowledge-based service businesses

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that most people can be shown they are resourceful when others depend on them (paying unexpected taxes, covering payroll) but choose not to be resourceful for themselves — and that pointing this out explicitly shifts the prospect's frame from 'I can't' to 'I choose not to'.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prospect is a business owner or has financial responsibilities to others
claims.mechanism: The proven ability to conjure money under external obligation reveals the constraint is motivational, not physical — surfacing this removes the prospect's ability to claim genuine inability.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that fit objections ('this vehicle isn't for me') are dissolved by the insight that stepping into a new identity requires adopting new priorities — and that people who want to become wealthy or healthy must begin spending time and money the way wealthy or healthy people do, because identity and spending/behavior are mutually constitutive.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prospect objects that the program's method doesn't match their current habits or preferences
claims.mechanism: Identity is performed through repeated resource allocation (money and time); adopting the spending and time patterns of a desired identity is itself the mechanism of identity formation.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that prospects who require spousal or partner approval before buying are asking for permission rather than support, and that the reframe — 'I'm not asking for permission, I'm asking for support' — is the correct frame because blaming the partner for withheld permission creates marital resentment when the goal is not achieved.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prospect cites absent spouse or partner as the reason they cannot decide on a results-based program
claims.mechanism: Framing the decision as 'permission' transfers ownership of the outcome to the partner. When the outcome fails, the partner is blamed. Framing it as 'support' restores the prospect's ownership of the decision and its results.
bounded_by: Applies when the absent partner is being used as a foil; does not apply when the purchase genuinely requires joint financial decision-making above a household threshold

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the avoidance objection ('I need to think about it') is almost always a proxy for incomplete information rather than a genuine need for time — because people believe they will gather more information during the thinking period, but if the seller is the only source of relevant information, additional time produces no new data.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prospect requests time to think after all substantive objections have been addressed
claims.mechanism: The 'think about it' request is based on an implicit assumption that time will bring information. Once the seller surfaces this assumption and establishes they are the sole information source, the prospect has no rational basis for delay.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the prospect has a legitimate need to consult an actual advisor (accountant, attorney) who holds material information the seller cannot provide

claims.text: Alex Hormozi proposes that the hypothetical close question — 'if this were perfect, would you do it?' — functions as a diagnostic: a 'no' answer reveals the real barrier is not program features but trust, which redirects the conversation to the actual issue; a 'yes' answer allows the seller to surface the gap between perfection and the current offer.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prospect is stalling or giving vague fit objections
claims.mechanism: The hypothetical question separates the prospect's belief in the category of solution from their concern about this specific implementation. A 'no' means category disbelief or trust failure; a 'yes' means a solvable product gap.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that with a guarantee in place, there are only three options available to a prospect: (1) do the thing and get the result, (2) don't do the thing and guarantee not getting the result, or (3) do the thing but not get the result — but with a refund guarantee, option 3 is risk-free. Only option 2 guarantees failure, making it the only truly risky choice.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: offer includes a satisfaction or money-back guarantee
bounded_by: Requires the guarantee to be genuine and honored; fails if the prospect does not trust the seller to honor refunds

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that fortunes are created by taking a lot of risk with a little money, and fortunes are maintained by taking a little risk with a lot of money — and that early-stage investors in themselves must take asymmetric risks on skill and education when capital is scarce.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: individual at early stage of wealth building
bounded_by: Does not apply to mature wealth preservation stage where capital protection becomes primary

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the ignorance tax — the annual cost of not knowing how to perform a skill — is the single largest unrecognized tax, exceeding income tax or capital gains, and that the cost of not knowing how to make a million dollars per year is itself a million dollars per year.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Ignorance of a value-producing skill means the income gap between current and potential earnings compounds annually; the forgone income is real whether or not it is perceived as a cost.

anchors.region: person who doesn't know how to generate $1M/year
person who doesn't know how to generate $1B/year

bounded_by: The analogy breaks down when income generation requires capital, not only skill

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that recording all sales calls serves two purposes: reviewing hot-streak recordings helps a salesperson return to peak state after a cold streak by identifying the specific behaviors (pauses, jokes, timing of close, objection handling) that drove performance; and hot-streak recordings are the most efficient training material for new salespeople.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: sales role with recurring phone or video conversations
claims.mechanism: Performance variance in sales is largely behavioral rather than skill-based; reviewing recorded hot-streak behavior makes the tacit explicit and allows deliberate replication.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the person who cares the most about the prospect's well-being will win the sale — including over the prospect themselves — because a seller with greater conviction about the prospect's need will cause the prospect to question the validity of their own excuses.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: consultative sales conversation
claims.mechanism: When a seller's certainty about an outcome exceeds the prospect's own certainty, the certainty gap creates cognitive dissonance in the prospect, causing them to re-evaluate the strength of their objections.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that emotional buyers who buy without rational foundation will call to reverse the decision within days, because when the initial emotion fades, the logic that would sustain the decision is absent — whereas a sale with rational grounding survives the emotional fade.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: high-ticket or considered purchase with a cooling-off period
claims.mechanism: Emotion reduces the action threshold and triggers the purchase; logic is the mechanism that sustains the decision once the emotion dissipates. Without logic, the decision has no structural support.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the reason he is effective at logical sales arguments is that he is inherently skeptical and used to paralyze himself without sound reasons to act — meaning the frameworks he uses to close prospects are the same frameworks he uses to make decisions for himself.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

examples.text: Alex Hormozi describes the Gym Launch experience where prospects would decline a $100 membership or challenge offer but then purchase $400 of supplements when invited to come back the next day for free help. He used this to learn that prospects must believe a product will achieve their goal *the way they want to get there* — not just that it will achieve the goal. The same person who wanted to lose weight rejected the gym format but accepted the supplement path.

Alex Hormozi tells a story about a CoachingCon audience member who challenged the definition of power. He defines power as the dictionary definition — the ability to influence or direct events or people — but contrasts it with a Confucian frame where omnipotence is the ideal (thought immediately becomes reality, with zero distance between intention and outcome). He uses this to argue that increasing power means shrinking the distance between decision and outcome.

Alex Hormozi describes watching two teenage girls at a Sephora makeup counter become excited about learning to use cosmetics. A store associate told them they now need to budget for makeup monthly as part of becoming a woman. Hormozi uses this to illustrate the new-identity / new-priorities mechanism: the girls instantly adopted new spending behavior because they adopted a new identity. He tells salespeople to use this logic with prospects who say the program method doesn't fit their current lifestyle.

Alex Hormozi recounts Phil Knight's Shoe Dog story: Nike was on the verge of collapse due to a capital gap that banks and lenders refused to fill. Knight's solution was to ask his vendors to fund payroll, treating suppliers as emergency credit facilities — a completely non-standard resourceful move. Hormozi uses this to illustrate that resourcefulness, not resources, is the distinguishing factor, and that self-made successes all started from zero.

Alex Hormozi recounts his own experience at age 22, flying unsolicited from Baltimore to Chino Hills, California to present himself to Sam Bakhtiar (Seven Figure Sam) after emailing 40 gym owners looking for a mentor. Bakhtiar called him a psychopath but then sold him a $10,000 gym mastermind — despite Hormozi not owning a gym and having limited funds. Hormozi credits this investment, which he was initially hesitant to make, as the inflection point that placed him on the path toward building a $100M business.

Alex Hormozi describes his father's contrast with his uncle. Both had wealth in Iran before the revolution. The uncle owned the Iranian lottery and had land, houses, and significant assets — all seized by the government. Hormozi's father came to the United States with $1,000 and a medical degree (skills), and rebuilt from scratch. The uncle relocated to London with no portable skills and still lives above a print shop. Hormozi uses this to argue that skills are the only non-seizable asset.

Alex Hormozi offers a personal example of how his wife once pulled out his phone and showed him 22 hours of social media usage in a single week — confronting his claim that he had no time. He uses this as a sales script: share the anecdote to help a prospect realize that time claimed to be absent is actually being consumed by low-value activity, and that the program would eliminate the activities making the prospect feel overwhelmed rather than adding to them.

Alex Hormozi uses a hypothetical joke close with a gym prospect to illustrate the authority/spousal objection override: 'If you sign up and your husband says he wants you to stay overweight, sit on the couch with Cheetos, and create generational unhealth — have him call me.' He uses humor to defuse the perceived partner veto and positions a three-day no-sweat guarantee as the safety valve that allows the prospect to sign without the partner's pre-authorization.

practices.text: Expect and plan for 'no' at the start of every sales conversation. Train new salespeople that 'no' is part of the job, not failure — if the prospect could decide yes on their own, they would have already sent the money.
Record all sales calls. When a cold streak hits, review recordings from the hot streak to identify specific behaviors (pause timing, jokes, close phrasing, objection handling) that can be replicated.

Ask hard questions with childlike curiosity during closing. When a prospect objects, respond with 'Huh, that's so weird — tell me more about that,' maintaining genuine curiosity rather than defensiveness.

Do not get stuck handling surface-level objections (time, money) without peeling toward the core. Use the three-distortion model — circumstances, others, self — to know which layer you are on and keep moving toward the prospect's real resistance.
Ask a prospect their single biggest fear about buying — 'What's the worst thing you envision happening?' — as one of the fastest ways to surface the real objection and move past proxy objections.

Use a satisfaction guarantee (3-day, 30-day) to allow prospects to make an informed decision from the inside, reframing the close as 'I'm not asking you to decide — I'm asking you to make an informed decision, which you can only do on the inside.'

Fill seller conviction before sales calls. If a team member's close rate drops without a change in skill, investigate what happened to their belief in the product — a negative customer interaction, a refund, a personal doubt — and address it directly before more training.

Invest aggressively in education and skill-building as the primary capital allocation in early career stages. Hormozi frames every course, coaching program, or mastermind as purchasing accumulated lessons from others' time spent, compounding faster than any financial asset.
